Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to design a Kubernetes-native control plane for secret lifecycle management, including external stores, safe rollouts, and auditable operations.

Key Concepts
- CustomResourceDefinition and operator pattern
- External secret stores (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, etc.)
- Canary validation and rollback strategy
- Observability: status, events, metrics
- RBAC scoping and secret access controls

Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: secretrotationpolicies.example.com
spec:
  group: example.com
  versions:
  - name: v1
    served: true
    storage: true
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          spec:
            type: object
            properties:
              schedule:
                type: string
              secretName:
                type: string
              namespace:
                type: string
  scope: Namespaced
  names:
    plural: secretrotationpolicies
    singular: secretrotationpolicy
    kind: SecretRotationPolicy
    shortNames: [srp]
```

Follow-up Questions

- What metrics and alerting would you implement to ensure rotation SLAs are met across many namespaces?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical exposure to Kubernetes networking end-to-end: services, ingress routing, DNS, and basic validation. It avoids high-level definitions and assesses concrete implementation decisions.

## Key Concepts
- Service types and port mappings
- Ingress routing rules and path types
- DNS resolution through CoreDNS and Ingress hostnames
- TLS termination basics with secrets

## Code Example
```yaml
# widget-svc.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: widget-svc
spec:
  selector:
    app: widget
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
```
```yaml
# widget-ingress.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: widget-ingress
  annotations:
    kubernetes.io/ingress.class: nginx
spec:
  tls:
  - hosts:
    - widget.example.com
    secretName: widget-tls
  rules:
  - host: widget.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /v1/*
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: widget-svc
            port:
              number: 80
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you enable mTLS between the Ingress and the service if needed?
- How do you monitor and verify health for the widget-svc and the Ingress routing rules?

## Why This Is Asked

Tests practical understanding of Deployment rollout behavior, readiness/liveness probes, and how to verify zero-downtime during a push.

## Key Concepts

- RollingUpdate strategy
- maxUnavailable and maxSurge semantics
- readinessProbe and livenessProbe configuration
- kubectl rollout status and rollout history for observability

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 2
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 0
      maxSurge: 1
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: your-image:tag
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 5
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 15
```

- How would you validate zero-downtime if the new image has longer startup?
- How would you handle a rollout failure and roll back?

questions.explanation:
A Pod is the fundamental building block of Kubernetes applications that represents a single running process in your cluster.

## Key Components
- **Containers**: One or more tightly coupled containers that work together
- **Shared Network**: All containers share the same IP address and network namespace
- **Shared Storage**: Access to shared volumes for data persistence and communication
- **Runtime Context**: Configuration for how containers should run together

## Why Smallest Deployable Unit?
- **Atomic Operation**: Pods are scheduled, created, and destroyed as a single unit
- **Resource Sharing**: Containers in a Pod can efficiently share resources via localhost
- **Co-location**: Ensures related processes run on the same node for performance
- **Lifecycle Management**: All containers in a Pod share the same fate (start/stop together)

## Common Use Cases
- **Single Container**: Most common scenario (web server, database)
- **Multi-Container**: Main app + sidecar proxy for logging/monitoring
- **Helper Processes**: Application + background worker processes

## Example YAML
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: web-app
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:latest
    ports:
    - containerPort: 80
  - name: log-agent
    image: fluentd:latest
    volumeMounts:
    - name: shared-logs
      mountPath: /var/log/nginx
```

## Why This Is Asked
Tests understanding of Kubernetes networking basics, NetworkPolicy syntax, and DNS vs IP-based rules, plus how to validate policies in a controlled pod.

## Key Concepts
- NetworkPolicy basics: policyTypes, podSelector, egress rules
- ipBlock vs DNS in policies; DNS names aren’t resolvable in policies
- Validation strategy: in-cluster test pod and basic curl checks

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: web-egress-deny
  namespace: web
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: web-api
  - to:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 203.0.113.0/24
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt this for per-namespace defaults with exceptions?
- How can you monitor violations and alert when policy changes cause connectivity failures?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

This question tests comprehensive knowledge of Kubernetes deployment strategies, particularly for hybrid workloads requiring zero-downtime while dealing with connection persistence and limited toolset constraints.

## Key Concepts

- Canary vs rolling update strategies for gradual traffic migration
- Service-based traffic splitting using labels and selectors
- Graceful connection termination with preStop hooks
- PodDisruptionBudgets for availability guarantees
- Readiness/Liveness probe configuration for deployment gating
- Rollback procedures using native kubectl commands
- Long-lived TCP connection handling during pod termination

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: production-app
spec:
  replicas: 20
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 10%
      maxSurge: 20%
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: frontend
        version: stable
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60
      containers:
      - name: app
        lifecycle:
          preStop:
            exec:
              command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 30"]
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 10
          periodSeconds: 5
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: production-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: frontend
    version: stable
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 8080
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you handle database schema changes during canary deployments?
- What monitoring signals would trigger automatic rollback?
- How would you implement this pattern for stateful services with persistent volumes?

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app

  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate

      maxUnavailable: 0
      maxSurge: 1

questions.explanation:
## Architecture
**Control Plane**: Pilot (traffic mgmt), Citadel (security), Galley (config validation)
**Data Plane**: Envoy sidecars intercept all inbound/outbound traffic

## Traffic Management
- VirtualService defines routing rules
- DestinationRule configures load balancing policies
- ServiceEntry for external services
- Circuit breaking, retries, timeouts

## Security
- mTLS via Citadel-managed certificates
- Authorization policies (RBAC)
- Secure service-to-service communication

## Observability
- Golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation
- Distributed tracing with Jaeger/Zipkin
- Metrics via Prometheus
- Access logs for audit trails

## Real-world Trade-offs
- **Performance**: ~3-5ms latency overhead per hop
- **Complexity**: Requires understanding of CRDs and networking concepts
- **Resource**: Additional 100-200MB memory per sidecar
